extracted.intended_audience: general readers and performers interested in impressionist entertainment (comedians, voice actors, historians)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for performing and evaluating celebrity/cartoon impressions — covering vocal technique, repertoire, use of props, caricature vs impersonation, and appropriate media/contexts. Geared to understanding the craft and historical/practical norms of impressionist entertainers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an impressionist/mimic
rubrics_metrics.description: An impressionist or a mimic is a performer whose act consists of imitating sounds, voices and mannerisms of celebrities and cartoon characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word usually refers to a professional comedian/entertainer who specializes in such performances and has developed a wide repertoire of impressions, including adding to them, often to keep pace with current events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocal fidelity (primary performance focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually the most 'impressive' aspect of the performance is the vocal fidelity to the target – usually a politician or a famous person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The voice is expected to carry the act; props may be used but are considered secondary. Vocal fidelity is often the key criterion by which an impressionist is judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repertoire breadth and topical updating
rubrics_metrics.description: Impressionists typically have developed a wide repertoire of impressions, including adding to them, often to keep pace with current events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad and up-to-date repertoire distinguishes an impressionist from a one-person impersonator; staying current with public figures and events helps maintain relevance and audience recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal reliance on props
rubrics_metrics.description: Props may also be employed, such as glasses or hats, but these are now considered somewhat old-fashioned and cumbersome: the voice is expected to carry the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of props is acceptable but should not substitute for vocal or behavioral accuracy; modern expectations favor vocal/mannerism skill over physical accessories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizability over exact replication (especially in animation/voice acting)
rubrics_metrics.description: With such indirect references, the entertainment value does not lie so much in the technical achievement of exactly reproducing the voice so much as in merely making it recognizable; the joke lies in the reference to a celebrity, not in its rendition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cartoons and some voice-acting contexts, evoking/recalling a celebrity is more important than perfect mimicry; clarity of reference serves the comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of distinctive mannerisms and visual shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctive mannerisms and dress can give performers visual shortcuts to cover for failings in their abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a target has conspicuous mannerisms or attire (example: Frank Spencer), leveraging those cues can help the audience instantly recognize the target even if some vocal or technical aspects are imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between impressionist and impersonator
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone who imitates one particular person without claiming a wide range, such as a lookalike, is instead called an impersonator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For labeling and positioning, reserve 'impressionist' for performers with a wide repertoire; use 'impersonator' for single-person specializations or lookalikes. In broad contexts 'impersonator' may substitute where confusion with the painting/music meaning of 'impressionist' is a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature versus faithful impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some shows/spoofs focus on making caricatures out of celebrities rather than impersonating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the act aims for caricature (exaggerated traits for comedic effect) or faithful impersonation (accuracy). Caricature emphasizes exaggeration and recognizable tropes; impersonation emphasizes likeness and fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized subskills (singing, animal/bird impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some impressionists have more specialized acts in the art; for example, some impersonate singing voices or do animal and bird impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialized niches (singing impersonations, bird/animal mimicry) require particular vocal technique and may be presented separately from general celebrity-voice impressions; they can distinguish an act and target different venues/audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate media and venue conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Impressionist performances are a classic casino entertainment genre and have been prominent on television, talent shows, sketch shows, and in animation/voice acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor material and technique to the venue: television and recorded media may reward breadth and topicality (e.g., political impressions), while live casino/variety shows may emphasize immediate recognizability and crowd-pleasing favorites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical and political emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Impressionists often focus on politicians and current public figures; political impressionists are a notable subcategory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political impressions can be influential in satire and public perception; maintaining accuracy, timeliness, and an awareness of the political context shapes audience reception and comedic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of historical and popular exemplars as benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent practitioners (e.g., Mike Yarwood, Rich Little, SNL cast members) serve as models of range, technique, and career pathways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying established impressionists provides examples of repertory size, vocal approaches, and how acts adapt to media and eras; these examples can be used as informal benchmarks for skill and career strategy.
